profile.headline: Quantum Computing | Astrophysics | Nuclear Fusion
profile.summary:
As a software engineer and data scientist I work with high-performing teams to develop cutting-edge software applications to solve a wide range of complex scientific and technical problems. Too vague? Interested in knowing more? Message me!

Prior to my career in data science and software development, I did doctoral research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research working at the intersection of theoretical and observational astrophysics. My research was in the field of cosmology, studying the large-scale structure and evolution of our Universe. Some of the tools I used included state-of-the-art, high-performance computer simulations and really, really big telescopes.

Before my work in astrophysics, I carried out doctoral research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Plasma Science and Fusion Center investigating the physics of plasmas and controlled nuclear fusion using the MIT Alcator C-Mod experimental tokamak reactor. My interest in fusion energy is motivated by the global need for a safe, sustainable energy source — the realization of which will be crucial for long-term human progress.

Outside of formal work, I enjoy spending time working on social issues including campaign finance reform, civic engagement, systemic institutional corruption, and existential risk (e.g., climate change, nuclear proliferation, and the ethics of artificial intelligence). Organizations I have collaborated with include the MIT Media Lab, Harvard Safra Center for Ethics, Harvard Kennedy School of Government, The Future of Life Institute, The High Impact Network, Represent.Us, Democracy Matters, Common Cause MA, Move to Amend Boston, Open Democracy, Demand Progress, and MassVOTE, in addition to other academic, political, legal, and technological organizations.

Do you have questions about black holes, dark matter, or multiverses? Interested in knowing more about how fusion reactors work (or why they don't)? Have an idea aligned with increasing social justice? Let's chat!

positions.title: Graduate Research Assistant - Astrophysics
positions.description: Theoretical and observational astrophysics research into cosmology, cosmic structure and reionization. My research focused on analyzing the spectra of high-z quasars to characterize the redshift evolution of metal abundances traced by ionic absorption lines. This effort mutually guided and informed cosmological simulations to constrain parameters responsible for galactic evolution and the ejection of metals into the circumgalactic and intergalactic mediums. In particular, placing limits on when the epoch of re-ionization occurred ending the cosmic "dark ages". Research advisors: Prof. Rob Simcoe (observational) & Prof. Mark Vogelsberger (theoretical).

positions.title: Graduate Teaching Assistant - Astrophysics I
positions.description: Taught weekly sections for the graduate course in astrophysics, held weekly office hours, and graded problem sets.

positions.title: Graduate Teaching Assistant - General Relativity
positions.description: Prepare and teach bi-weekly sections for the graduate course in General Relativity (Einstein's elegant, description of gravity as the geometric curvature of spacetime – and a top three contender for my favorite theory). In addition, I held weekly office hours and developed problems and solutions to homework, as well as grading assignments. Gave a special lecture on the theory of cosmic inflation.

positions.title: Graduate Research Assistant - Plasma Physics
positions.description: Experimental plasma physics and controlled nuclear fusion research on the MIT Alcator C-Mod experimental tokamak reactor. My research focused on the measurement and characterization of impurity sources at the plasma "edge" of tokamak fusion devices. In particular, I have studied the impurity transport at the "outer limiter" and divertor, critical components in current and future tokamak devices. Spectroscopy was my primary diagnostic tool, and I designed and assembled custom spectrographs optimized for very high-throughput to study plasma discharges. Research advisor: Prof. Bruce Lipschultz

positions.title: Mathematics Teaching Assistant
positions.description: Teaching assistant for the mathematics course “Introduction to Bayesian Inference"..

company.name: The University of Texas at Austin

positions.title: Undergraduate Teaching Assistant - Electromagnetism
positions.description: Prepared and conducted weekly discussion sections for the Electricity and Magnetism course for undergraduate physics majors. In my discussion sections, I introduced alternative viewpoints and approaches to canonical problems in an effort to help students move past superficial familiarity and gain a more meaningful understanding of electromagnetic phenomena. I was invited to give guest lectures and commended for "superb teaching performance" by Prof. Richard Hazeltine.

positions.title: Undergraduate Research Assistant - Astrophysics
positions.description: Computational astrophysics. The focus of my research was to model the radial number density of Population III (the very first) stars and their remnant massive black holes (BH) in galactic dark matter halos as a function of cosmological redshift. I applied a semi-analytical approach (Press-Schecter formalism) to model PopIII stellar evolution and place constraints on the progenitor sub-halos where the massive first stars formed. Based on the results, I was able to calculate the fraction of PopIII BHs captured by the super-massive black holes at the center of galaxies as a function of cosmological redshift. And for the fraction of Pop III stars that didn't collapse into black holes, I calculated the horizons of observability where their electromagnetic and gravitational radiation signatures could be detected. Research advisor: Prof. Volker Bromm

positions.title: Undergraduate Research Assistant - Electromagnetic Braking
positions.description: Independent table-top physics investigation of electromagnetic braking. In this project I worked toward an analytical formula describing the terminal velocities of cylindrical (neodymium) magnets falling though (non-magnetic) conducting tubes, with parameters including magnetic field strength, tube inner-diameter, wall thickness, and conductivity. I designed, purchased, and machined all the experimental apparatus including a photo-gate circuit that could quickly and easily accomodate the variation in tube geometrical parameters. Research advisor: Prof. Peter Antoniewicz

positions.title: Undergraduate Research Assistant - Plasma Physics
positions.description: Experimental plasma physics research on the Helimak device. My primary research project was concerned with measurement of the high energy tail of the electron energy distribution function. To accomplish this I designed, constructed, and installed an electrostatic velocity analyzer in the Helimak device. The results and analyses of data collected with the velocity analyzer formed the topic of my honors thesis. Research advisor: Prof. Ken Gentle

positions.title: Physics and Mathematics Tutor
positions.description: Proposed and initiated a physics and mathematics tutoring service for the UT Austin Center for Students in Recovery. Tutored university students in physics and mathematics courses ranging from Newtonian mechanics and college algebra to quantum mechanics and partial differential equations. Commended for my commitment to the students, specifically for my effort in tailoring my teaching methods to meet each student's individual circumstance.

positions.title: Stanley Scholar Medical Research Assistant
positions.description: Schizophrenia, schizoaffective, and schizophreniform disorder research. I took part in an exhaustive literature search for randomized, double-blind clinical trials of second generation antipsychotics in the treatment of schizophrenia. I was heavily involved with both the data aquisition and statistical analysis performed in a meta-analysis of the literature search to quantify how bias is introduced into industry-funded clinical trials compared to non-industry funded trials, the results of which are published in the article, "An analysis of the effect of funding source in randomized clinical trials of second generation antipsychotics for the treatment of schizophrenia". In addition to research, I gained hands-on experience in the clinical treatment of persons affected with schizophrenia, sitting in on clinical appointments and even participating in patient sessions when deemed safe and appropriate. Principle Researcher: Dr. Matthew Byerly

At the FLI, I was a volunteer in research projects, the social media manager, and had the privilege of helping this wonderful organization at its founding.

THINK is an organization that promotes effective altruism. With creativity, strategy and intellectual rigor, members collaborate to dramatically increase their impact on the world. As an officer of the MIT student group THINK, I was the lead organizer of a 3-day event comprised of an 800+ attendee symposium, followed by a 2-day long hackathon where over 50 participants worked in groups to develop real tools in real time.
The symposium, "Citizens Rising", aimed to provide an understanding of campaign finance reform and its role in political inequality, as well as presenting audience members with an array of direct actions through which individuals may immediately begin affecting political change.
The 2-day hackathon, "Hack for Democracy – Boston", was held at the MIT Stata Center and brought together ambitious participants with a wide range of expertise including law, medicine, fine arts, political science, astrophysics, and of course software engineering and coding. Ten teams presented their group projects offering legislation, technology-assisted social engagement, and other tech-y solutions aimed at improving American democracy.

projects.title: #Hack4Congress – Harvard Kennedy School & OpenGov Foundation
projects.description:
Hackathon participant and project winner of the Campaign Finance Reform challenge at the Harvard Kennedy School and the OpenGov Foundation’s Hackathon, #Hack4Congress. The 3-day hackathon focused on improving aspects of American democracy with multidisciplinary team projects aimed at identifying and creating innovative methods to overcome the dysfunction gripping much of Congress.

projects.title: Hacking iCorruption - Harvard Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics & MIT Media Lab
projects.description:
Organizer and MC of a 3-day long speaker panel and hackathon event sponsored by the Harvard Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics in collaboration with the MIT Media Lab Center for Civic Media. This multidisciplinary event aimed to develop novel methods to fix the systemic, legal corruption that is weakening our public institutions around the world.
